To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) Peirce's retroduction is a form of inference to the best explanation, and is not a fallible form of deduction; (2) Peirce conceived of deduction as divided into two sub stages, logical analysis and mathematical deduction; and (3) mathematical deduction can be either corollarial (i.e., deductive reasoning) or theorematic (i.e., inductive reasoning)

(1) Peirce's conception of retroduction, as it is developed in his late manuscripts, is that of a non-deductive, non-inductive, and yet valid inference, and that it is the only kind of inference that can lead from the known to the unknown; and (2) that Peirce's notion of scientific reasoning is a complex one, which involves three distinct kinds of inferences, two of which are deductive and one of which is retroduction.

(a) Peirce's conception of retroduction is a form of inference to the best explanation, and that (b) his later conception of deduction is a form of mathematical reasoning, which is either corollarially or theorematically justified.
In summary, our research is concerned with
Peirce's views on the logic and methodology of science and reasoning, and with the logical structure and the epistemological status of retroduction and deduction.

the following questions. What is retroduction? What is the logic of scientific inquiry, and what is its relation to logic? How does Peirce conceive the logic of science in his late writings, and how do they differ from his earlier conceptions?

the following questions: (i) What is the logical status of retroduction? (ii) Is retroduction a genuine form of inference? (iii) Is retroduction an inductive form of inference? and (iv) How does Peirce's conception of deduction compare with his earlier conception of the subject?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the logic of science is a logic of abduction, deduction, and inductive generalization.
the logic of science as conceived by Peirce was a logic of reasoning, not a logic of proof or demonstration.

the logical structure of scientific reasoning is not a simple triadic process, but a fourfold process, in which retroduction, corollarial and theorematical deduction are the first three stages, followed by a fourth stage, which is theorematical mathematical reasoning.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Peirce's logic of scientific reasoning is a three-stage procedure, which includes abduction, corollarial analysis, and corollarial mathematical reasoning.
the logic of scientific reasoning is not a logic of propositions, nor is it a logic of concepts.

Peirce's views on the logic and methodology of science underwent significant changes during his late years, and that his later conceptions of the three stages of inquiry and of the two sub stages of deduction are more coherent and more systematic than his earlier views.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the logical form of Peirce s conception of retroduction is not a matter of abduction but rather of induction.

Peirce's logic of science, and especially his late conception of retroduc- tion, has been misunderstood and misrepresented in the secondary literature, and that a careful study of Peirce s late work shows that he was not a fallibilist in the Popperian or Kuhnian sense, but rather a fallibilist of a more modest kind.

Peirce's conception of retroduction, deduction and scientific reasoning, as developed in his later work, is more complex and nuanced than has been generally acknowledged, and that it is also more in line with the spirit of the modern philosophy of science.
